extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Cervantes / readers of classic literature
extracted.subtask_description: Passage from Don Quixote in which Don Quixote gives Sancho Panza a lengthy set of precepts about governing an island, covering moral duties, personal comportment, domestic management, and judicial conduct. The text is prescriptive within the fictional narrative and functions as a set of behavioral and ethical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear God
rubrics_metrics.description: “First of all, my son, thou must fear God, for in the fear of him is wisdom...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as foundational moral advice: fearing God produces wisdom and prevents error in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: “Secondly, thou must keep in view what thou art, striving to know thyself, the most difficult thing to know that the mind can imagine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-knowledge will prevent pride and ill-judged ambition (example: avoid puffing up like the frog that strove to make himself as large as the ox).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany dignity with gentle suavity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who are not of noble origin should take care that the dignity of the office they hold be accompanied by a gentle suavity, which wisely managed will save them from the sneers of malice…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one lacks noble birth, manage office with courtesy and tact to avoid ridicule; comportment can compensate for low origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory in humble birth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Glory in thy humble birth, Sancho, and be not ashamed of saying thou art peasant-born; for when it is seen thou art not ashamed no one will set himself to put thee to the blush…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages pride in honest origins as a defense against social shame or attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value virtue over blood
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pride thyself rather upon being one of lowly virtue than a lofty sinner. Blood is an inheritance, but virtue an acquisition…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral worth (virtue) counts more than noble lineage; governs decisions and reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcome visiting kinsfolk
rubrics_metrics.description: “If perchance anyone of thy kinsfolk should come to see thee when thou art in thine island, thou art not to repel or slight him, but on the contrary to welcome him, entertain him, and make much of him…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hospitality towards kin is morally approved and conforms to natural/social law; avoid disdain.

rubrics_metrics.name: If thou carriest thy wife, instruct her
rubrics_metrics.description: “If thou carriest thy wife with thee … teach and instruct her, and strive to smooth down her natural roughness; for all that may be gained by a wise governor may be lost and wasted by a boorish stupid wife.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic management: a governor should guide and civilize a spouse to avoid social/political harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a consort wisely (not for utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If perchance thou art left a widower … choose not one to serve thee for a hook, or for a fishing-rod, or for the hood of thy ‘won’t have it;’ …”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advises against selecting a spouse solely for instrumental or cosmetic reasons; choose on more appropriate grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary law
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never go by arbitrary law, which is so much favoured by ignorant men who plume themselves on cleverness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abjures capricious rulings and favoritism; decisions should be lawful and reasoned, not arbitrary cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show compassion to the poor (but preserve justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let the tears of the poor man find with thee more compassion, but not more justice, than the pleadings of the rich.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize compassionate reception of the poor while maintaining impartial justice; do not privilege wealth over need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the truth beyond gifts and sobs
rubrics_metrics.description: “Strive to lay bare the truth, as well amid the promises and presents of the rich man, as amid the sobs and entreaties of the poor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate facts without being misled by wealth, gifts, or emotional displays; truth-seeking is essential to fair governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer mercy to excessive rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: “When equity may and should be brought into play, press not the utmost rigour of the law against the guilty; for the reputation of the stern judge stands not higher than that of the compassionate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When equitable considerations apply, temper strict legal penalties with mercy; compassion enhances reputation more than severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let mercy, not gifts, sway justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “If perchance thou permittest the staff of justice to swerve, let it be not by the weight of a gift, but by that of mercy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposes corruption: any deviation from strict law should be for humane reasons, never because of bribery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias when judging enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: “If it should happen to thee to give judgment in the cause of one who is thine enemy, turn thy thoughts away from thy injury and fix them on the justice of the case.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction to set aside personal grievances and decide impartially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let passion blind thee
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let not thine own passion blind thee in another man’s cause; for the errors thou wilt thus commit will be most frequently irremediable…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional involvement leads to serious, often irreversible mistakes; cultivate detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unswayed by beauty when dispensing justice
rubrics_metrics.description: “If any handsome woman come to seek justice of thee, turn away thine eyes from her tears and thine ears from her lamentations, and consider deliberately the merits of her demand…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against allowing physical attractiveness or sentiment to influence legal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not verbally abuse those you punish
rubrics_metrics.description: “Abuse not by word him whom thou hast to punish in deed, for the pain of punishment is enough for the unfortunate without the addition of thine objurgations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous verbal humiliation; punishment should not be compounded with insult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bear in mind the culprit’s misery; be lenient
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bear in mind that the culprit who comes under thy jurisdiction is but a miserable man subject to all the propensities of our depraved nature, and so far as may be in thy power show thyself lenient and forbearing…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize human frailty; apply leniency and forbearance where possible—mercy is exalted above justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clean and trim nails
rubrics_metrics.description: “With regard to the mode in which thou shouldst govern thy person and thy house, Sancho, the first charge I have to give thee is to be clean, and to cut thy nails, not letting them grow as some do…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal hygiene is a sign of propriety and competence; neglect is a social liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disordered attire
rubrics_metrics.description: “Go not ungirt and loose, Sancho; for disordered attire is a sign of an unstable mind, unless indeed the slovenliness and slackness is to be set down to craft…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress that appears careless signals instability; unless slovenliness is an intentional affectation for purpose, presentability matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain office's means; clothe servants and poor
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ascertain cautiously what thy office may be worth; and if it will allow thee to give liveries to thy servants, give them respectable and serviceable, rather than showy and gay ones, and divide them between thy servants and the poor…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resources realistically; favor practical, respectable displays and share benefits with the needy—charity alongside dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid garlic and onions (avoid revealing boorish origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Eat not garlic nor onions, lest they find out thy boorish origin by the smell;”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical social advice: avoid foods that betray lowly origins or offend company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk slowly and speak deliberately; avoid affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Walk slowly and speak deliberately, but not in such a way as to make it seem thou art listening to thyself, for all affectation is bad.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured deportment fosters respect; avoid affected mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in eating and drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dine sparingly and sup more sparingly still; for the health of the whole body is forged in the workshop of the stomach. Be temperate in drinking, bearing in mind that wine in excess keeps neither secrets nor promises.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes temperance: health and prudence derive from moderation; excess undermines discretion and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No chewing on both sides; no belching in company
rubrics_metrics.description: “Take care, Sancho, not to chew on both sides, and not to eruct in anybody’s presence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table manners: avoid vulgar actions (Don Quixote recommends using the Latin 'eruct' as a euphemism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proverbs sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thou must not mingle such a quantity of proverbs in thy discourse as thou dost; … I do not say that a proverb aptly brought in is objectionable; but to pile up and string together proverbs at random makes conversation dull and vulgar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proverbs have rhetorical value if used aptl y; overuse makes discourse foolish and coarse—avoid excessive proverbial speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt proper riding posture
rubrics_metrics.description: “When thou ridest on horseback, do not go lolling with thy body on the back of the saddle, nor carry thy legs stiff or sticking out from the horse’s belly, nor yet sit so loosely that one would suppose thou wert on Dapple; for the seat on a horse makes gentlemen of some and grooms of others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical comportment on horse signals social status; proper posture distinguishes a gentleman/governor from a groom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be moderate in sleep; rise early; diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Be moderate in thy sleep; for he who does not rise early does not get the benefit of the day; and remember, Sancho, diligence is the mother of good fortune, and indolence, its opposite, never yet attained the object of an honest ambition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work ethic advice: early rising and diligence are prerequisites for success in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes comparing families
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never engage in a dispute about families, at least in the way of comparing them one with another; for necessarily one of those compared will be better than the other, and thou wilt be hated by the one thou hast disparaged…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political prudence: avoid needlessly inflaming factions by comparing family status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate governor attire
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thy attire shall be hose of full length, a long jerkin, and a cloak a trifle longer; loose breeches by no means, for they are becoming neither for gentlemen nor for governors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific sartorial prescription: certain garments signal the dignity of office; avoid loose breeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to read or at least to sign your name
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a great defect that thou labourest under, and therefore I would have thee learn at any rate to sign thy name.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literacy (or ability to sign) is presented as important for a governor; illiteracy is criticized as a social defect.
